content: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a genetic disorder that requires strict dietary management, specifically the restriction of the amino acid phenylalanine. This dietary intervention must begin during the neonatal period to prevent or mitigate intellectual disabilities. However, the prescribed diet is highly restrictive, often unpalatable, and challenging to adhere to over time. A deficiency in the amino acid tyrosine has been proposed as a potential contributor to some of the neuropsychological issues observed in individuals with PKU. Consequently, this review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of tyrosine supplementation as a therapeutic strategy for PKU. This review represents an update of previously published versions. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether tyrosine supplementation, either in conjunction with or as a replacement for a phenylalanine-restricted diet, has beneficial effects on individuals with PKU. Specifically, the review aimed to assess whether tyrosine supplementation improves cognitive function, neuropsychological performance, physical growth, nutritional status, mortality rates, and overall quality of life. The review focused on individuals who began dietary management at the time of diagnosis and either continued the diet or relaxed it later in life. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Trials Register. This register includes references from extensive electronic database searches, manual searches of pertinent journals, and conference abstract books. Additional studies were identified through manual searches of the Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease (from its inception in 1978 to 1998). Manufacturers of dietary products used in PKU management were also contacted for further references. The most recent search of the Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register was conducted on December 7, 2020. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated the use of tyrosine supplementation compared to placebo in individuals with PKU, either in addition to or as a substitute for a phenylalanine-restricted diet. Studies involving maternal PKU were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and methodological quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. Six trials were identified, but only three trials, involving a total of 56 participants, met the inclusion criteria for the review. Participants who received tyrosine supplementation demonstrated significantly higher blood tyrosine concentrations compared to those in the placebo group, with a mean difference of 23.46 (95% confidence interval: 12.87 to 34.05). However, no significant differences were observed in any of the other measured outcomes, including cognitive function, neuropsychological performance, growth, nutritional status, mortality, or quality of life. The included trials were assessed as having a low to moderate risk of bias across several methodological domains. Based on the available evidence, no definitive recommendations can be made regarding the routine clinical use of tyrosine supplementation in the management of PKU. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to provide more robust evidence. However, given the lack of ongoing research in this area, there are no plans to update this review in the future.
